pharm: A poorly absorbed iodinated 8-hydroxyquinoline that acts locally in the gut lumen against Entamoeba histolytica, eradicating cyst-passing and trophozoites in the intestinal lumen; precise mechanism is not fully defined but likely involves chelation of metal ions needed by the parasite.

Take after meals; tablets may be crushed and mixed with applesauce/chocolate syrup
Use only if clearly needed; contains iodine
Caution - iodine may be excreted in milk and affect infant thyroid
Thyroid function (iodine), ophthalmologic exam if prolonged/high-dose use (optic neuropathy)
summary: Di-iodohydroxyquinoline (iodoquinol) is an oral, poorly absorbed luminal amebicide used to treat intestinal amebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica), typically as a follow-on after a tissue amebicide such as metronidazole to eradicate luminal cysts. It is also used for asymptomatic cyst passers. Because it acts within the intestinal lumen, it is not effective alone for extraintestinal (e.g. hepatic) amebiasis. It is an iodine-containing compound, so it can interfere with thyroid function tests for months and is contraindicated in iodine intolerance and hepatic damage. The most important historical toxicity is subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) and optic atrophy/peripheral neuropathy reported with high doses or prolonged use of related hydroxyquinolines, so the labeled dose and duration must not be exceeded. It is FDA-recognized for amebiasis.
indications: Adjunct to a tissue amebicide (e.g. metronidazole) to eradicate intraluminal cysts after treatment of invasive disease

Tablets may be crushed and mixed with a small amount of applesauce or chocolate syrup for patients who cannot swallow them

moa: Di-iodohydroxyquinoline is a halogenated 8-hydroxyquinoline that acts as a contact (luminal) amebicide within the intestinal lumen, where it is effective against the trophozoite and cyst forms of Entamoeba histolytica. Its precise antiprotozoal mechanism has not been fully established but is thought to involve chelation of ferrous and other metal ions required for parasite enzyme/metabolic function. Because it is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, high local concentrations are achieved in the bowel lumen, which accounts for its efficacy against luminal organisms and its lack of effect against tissue (extraintestinal) amebiasis.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to iodoquinol/8-hydroxyquinolines or to iodine-containing compounds
monitor: Visual function with prolonged therapy (optic neuropathy)

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. The drug contains iodine, which crosses the placenta. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: Iodine is excreted in human milk and could affect the nursing infant's thyroid. Caution should be exercised when iodoquinol is administered to a breastfeeding woman; weigh benefit against potential infant effects.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is provided; the drug is poorly absorbed and acts locally in the gut. Use with caution in renal disease.
hepatic: Contraindicated in patients with hepatic damage. The drug is not appropriate for hepatic (extraintestinal) amebiasis as it is a luminal agent only.

moderate: Iodine-containing diagnostic agents / thyroid function testing - iodoquinol can elevate protein-bound iodine and interfere with thyroid tests for up to several months
interactions.food: Take after meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset; food does not significantly impair efficacy of this luminal agent.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with alcohol is described.
interactions.diagnostics: Contains iodine and can increase protein-bound serum iodine, interfering with certain thyroid function tests (and possibly thyroid radioiodine uptake) for weeks to months after therapy.

serious: Optic neuritis, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy (subacute myelo-optic neuropathy, SMON) - with high doses or prolonged use
rare: Iodism (metallic taste, sore gums, skin eruptions, salivary gland swelling)
emergency: Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy with high-dose/prolonged use

monitoring: Ophthalmologic examination if therapy is prolonged or doses are high (optic neuropathy)
Thyroid function tests (recognizing iodine-related test interference)
Follow-up stool examinations to confirm parasitologic cure
Symptoms and signs of neuropathy (visual changes, paresthesias, weakness)
Skin and mucosa for signs of iodism or hypersensitivity
counsel: Take this medicine after meals and finish the full 20-day course exactly as prescribed
Do not take more than prescribed or for longer than directed - high or prolonged doses can damage the optic and peripheral nerves
Tell your doctor right away if you have any change in vision, numbness, or weakness in the limbs
This medicine contains iodine and can affect thyroid blood tests for a few months - remind any doctor ordering thyroid tests
If you cannot swallow the tablet, it can be crushed and mixed with applesauce or chocolate syrup
Report rash, persistent diarrhea, or itching around the anus
pk: Acts locally in the gut lumen during the treatment course
Limited systemic data due to poor absorption; absorbed fraction excreted in urine
Acts throughout the 20-day course; iodine effects on thyroid tests persist weeks-months
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Luminal (contact) amebicide - eradicates intestinal cysts but is NOT effective for hepatic/extraintestinal amebiasis; pair with a tissue agent like metronidazole
It is an FDA-recognized drug for amebiasis (iodoquinol)
Iodine-containing - interferes with thyroid function tests for up to several months
Do not exceed the labeled dose/duration: high-dose or prolonged related hydroxyquinoline use caused subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) and optic atrophy
Contraindicated in hepatic damage and iodine hypersensitivity
Allow a 2-3 week interval before repeating a course
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule - do not take a double dose. Complete the full prescribed course even if you feel better.
overdose: Acute overdose data are limited. Excessive or prolonged dosing is associated with optic and peripheral neuropathy and iodism. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with discontinuation of the drug and symptomatic care. Obtain ophthalmologic and neurologic evaluation if toxicity is suspected.
